outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Deixis and anaphora.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: Reference determined by features of the utterance-act, such as speaker, addressee, time and place.
An expression whose reference is fixed in relation to the utterance-act.
The word within a larger expression that carries the deictic meaning.
A gesture, gaze or written device that helps identify a deictic referent.
The perspective from which deictic expressions are interpreted, usually the speaker’s.
Deixis involving the speaker, addressee or third parties, expressed by personal pronouns.
Deixis of place, expressed by here, there, this, that and related expressions.
Deixis of time, expressed by now, then, yesterday and tense.
The relation in which an expression receives its interpretation from an antecedent.
An expression interpreted through an antecedent.
The expression that supplies the interpretation of an anaphor.
Anaphora in which the anaphor follows its antecedent.
Anaphora in which the anaphor precedes its antecedent.
A reduced expression that stands for a larger expression or clause.
A form such as herself or themselves used for local anaphora or emphasis.
A form such as each other or one another expressing a mutual relation.
A determinative or pronoun such as this or that used for deixis or anaphora.
The pronoun one used to stand for a nominal expression.
An expression that performs the head function together with a dependent function.
Omission of material that is recoverable from context.
Use of an auxiliary alone as a reduced predicate, as in I could.
A pro-form replacing a verb phrase, as in She left and I did so too.
A pro-form with a pronoun object, often referring to a specific action.
So used as a pro-form for a clause or proposition.
Ellipsis of a repeated verb in a coordination, as in Kim likes tea and Pat coffee.
Deixis of location and movement, as with here, there, come and go.
Interpretation of a time expression through an antecedent time in the discourse.
A shift of the deictic perspective from speaker to addressee or a reported participant.
A pronoun used for people in general rather than a specific referent, as in You can’t tell.

options.feedback: Here is interpreted relative to the speaker’s location.
Paris has a place-based meaning independent of the utterance.
That is a non-deictic temporal expression.

options.text: An expression that supplies the interpretation of an anaphor
options.feedback: Max is the antecedent of he in Max claims he was tired.
That is a different concept.
A pro-form is the anaphoric expression, not the antecedent.
Generic you refers to people in general.
That refers to the addressee.
That is third person anaphoric.

options.text: When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police.
options.feedback: The pronoun precedes the headmaster.

options.text: When the headmaster saw the damage, he called the police.
options.feedback: That is retrospective.
There is no anaphor.
She left and I did so too.
Pro-nominal one replaces an NP.
Do so is a VP pro-form.

closing.prompt: Why is here deictic but Paris is not?

options.text: Here is interpreted relative to the utterance place; Paris is not.
options.feedback: Deictic meaning is tied to the utterance-act.

options.text: Paris is a proper name and proper names are never deictic.
options.feedback: Proper names can be used deictically, but their meaning is not utterance-anchored.
Here is not a preposition.

options.text: Anaphora in which the anaphor precedes its antecedent
options.feedback: When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police.

options.text: Anaphora in which the antecedent is omitted
options.feedback: The antecedent is present later.
That is person deixis.

closing.prompt: Which use of it has no referent?

options.text: Dummy it in It is clear that he’s guilty
options.feedback: It fills the subject position but does not refer.

options.text: Anaphoric it in I found the key and put it in my pocket
options.feedback: It refers to the key.
It is non-referential, but the question targets the dummy use.

options.text: A mutual relation among members of a group
options.feedback: They helped each other.

options.text: A reflexive relation with a singular antecedent
options.feedback: Reciprocals require a plural or group antecedent.

options.text: A deictic relation to the speaker
options.feedback: Reciprocals are anaphoric.

closing.prompt: What does do so replace in She left and I did so too?

options.feedback: Do so stands for the predicate.
The second subject is I.
It replaces the predicate.
